title: 100-Day Plan
summary: The 100-Day Plan explains how sponsors convert transaction momentum into immediate operating control.
definition: A 100-Day Plan is the post-close execution sprint that establishes governance, validates the thesis, captures early wins, and sets the operating cadence.
whyItMatters: PE operators use the first 100 days to prevent drift, expose surprises, stabilize cash, and prove that the value creation plan can survive contact with reality.
example: A sponsor may launch cash controls, KPI reporting, management assessment, pricing cleanup, and procurement quick wins before the first full board cycle.

articleSections.title: Translate the Mandate into an Operating Thesis
body: The 100-day plan is the first controlled test of the acquisition mandate. It converts the IC thesis—why this asset, why now, and why this owner—into a finite set of operating outcomes that management can deliver. The mandate should identify the earnings baseline, the two or three value levers that justify the investment, the risks that could impair debt service, and the capabilities required for the next phase. Without that hierarchy, the plan becomes a catalogue of sensible projects with no relationship to returns.

The sponsor and CEO should align before close on what must be true by day 100. Typical proof points include a trusted weekly flash, a stable 13-week cash forecast, validated initiative economics, confirmed leadership roles, and the first measured benefits in the P&L. The plan is not expected to complete a three-year transformation. It is expected to remove the uncertainties that prevent the board from committing resources and to demonstrate that the company can operate at the cadence assumed in underwriting.

Ownership matters because a sponsor mandate is not an operating instruction until named executives accept it. The deal partner owns fidelity to the investment case, the operating partner owns translation into executable work, the CEO owns enterprise trade-offs, and functional leaders own delivery. If the pricing thesis requires better customer-level data, the CFO and commercial leader jointly own the baseline before the sales team owns rollout. That sequencing prevents management from being held accountable for economics the company cannot yet measure.
articleSections.callout: Day 100 is a proof gate: the sponsor should know which thesis levers are real, who can deliver them, and what resources the hold-period plan requires.

articleSections.title: Convert Diligence Findings into Workable Initiatives
body: Diligence observations must be rewritten as initiatives with a baseline, action, owner, timing, cost, and measurable financial outcome. A commercial report that says discounting is inconsistent is only a hypothesis. The translation specifies which customer segments will be repriced, how elasticity will be tested, when contracts permit action, and how gross-to-net realization will be measured. The same discipline applies to procurement, labor productivity, working capital, and systems: evidence becomes a workstream only after management can explain how the operational change reaches EBITDA or cash.

Translation also reconciles competing baselines. The QoE may report $18 million of adjusted EBITDA, the lender model may use $17 million, and management's budget may start from $19 million. Before initiative value is claimed, the CFO must build a bridge among reported results, permitted covenant EBITDA, and the operating baseline. Otherwise a $2 million savings program can appear successful while total earnings miss because volume, mix, or stranded cost moved in the opposite direction. Baseline governance is a day-one control, not a finance clean-up deferred to quarter end.

Each initiative should carry explicit diligence dependencies and kill criteria. A procurement opportunity may depend on clean spend cubes, supplier termination rights, and no adverse quality effect. A sales-force redesign may depend on territory data, account coverage, and a leader capable of enforcing new incentives. If the evidence fails, the owner either redesigns the intervention or removes the benefit from the plan; the sponsor does not keep an underwritten number alive through optimistic status labels. This honesty preserves credibility when the plan is handed to the board.

articleSections.title: Prioritize by Value, Certainty, and Organizational Capacity
body: Prioritization is a capital-allocation exercise, not a vote among functions. Initiatives should be scored on expected EBITDA or cash impact, confidence in the baseline, time to first benefit, investment required, reversibility, and demand on scarce leaders. Cash controls, pricing leakage, overtime, and vendor terms often lead because they are measurable and can self-fund later work. ERP replacement, site consolidation, or channel expansion may be essential, but launching all three during leadership assessment creates execution congestion and raises the probability that no workstream reaches a decision gate.

Consider a $120 million revenue distributor with $12 million of entry EBITDA. The plan identifies $1.5 million from price realization, $1.2 million from sourcing, and $0.8 million from warehouse productivity, offset by $0.7 million of recurring commercial and analytics hires. The gross bridge is $3.5 million; the net run-rate bridge is $2.8 million, taking EBITDA to $14.8 million before market growth. At a 10x exit multiple, that improvement can support $28 million of enterprise value, but only if owners distinguish signed, implemented, realized, and annualized benefit.

Sequence the bridge so proof finances ambition. In days 1–30, stabilize cash, validate customer and SKU economics, and lock decision rights. In days 31–60, pilot price and sourcing actions while assessing leadership and systems constraints. In days 61–100, scale successful pilots, stop weak ones, and fund longer-horizon capabilities. A gate should require both operational evidence and financial reconciliation: a price increase is not complete when letters are sent, but when invoices, retention, volume, and gross margin show the intended net effect.

articleSections.title: Install Governance and a Weekly Execution Cadence
body: The weekly 100-day review is a decision forum, not a presentation meeting. A transformation lead maintains the integrated plan; initiative owners report milestone evidence, economic realization, dependencies, and decisions required. The CEO resolves cross-functional conflicts, the CFO certifies benefit accounting and cash impact, and the operating partner challenges pace and removes sponsor-controlled barriers. A concise red-amber-green view is useful only when status follows rules: missed critical-path milestone, unvalidated economics, or absent owner means red regardless of narrative confidence.

Cadence should run at several speeds. A Monday flash covers sales, service, labor, liquidity, and immediate exceptions. The weekly initiative review governs the plan-to-EBITDA bridge. The monthly operating review reconciles full financial performance, covenant outlook, and resource allocation. The board receives a decision-oriented synthesis rather than the raw project log. Matters such as executive changes, material capex, covenant risk, or a thesis-lever failure escalate immediately instead of waiting for the next calendar meeting.

Common failure modes are visible early: too many initiatives, benefits counted before they hit invoices or payroll, owners without authority, and sponsor teams bypassing the CEO. Another is confusing activity with control—dozens of workshops can coexist with an unreliable close and no cash forecast. The response is subtraction and clarity. Stop low-value work, assign one accountable owner per outcome, tighten benefit definitions, and reserve executive attention for constraints that threaten the value bridge or the ability to service debt.

articleSections.title: Use Day 100 as the Hold-Period Handoff Gate
body: At day 100, the board should review evidence against the original mandate, not celebrate completion of a checklist. The package should show the reconciled earnings baseline, initiative-level gross and net benefits, cash and covenant trajectory, leadership conclusions, system and capability gaps, and decisions requested for the next twelve months. Every underwritten lever is classified as confirmed, revised, deferred, or rejected. This creates an auditable transition from transaction assumptions to an operating forecast owned by management.

The handoff converts pilots into the multi-year value creation plan. Confirmed initiatives receive quarterly milestones, budgets, and executive incentives; unresolved hypotheses receive bounded tests and expiration dates; rejected ideas come out of the case. In the distributor example, perhaps $0.9 million of pricing and $0.7 million of sourcing are already annualizing, while warehouse productivity needs a $0.4 million systems investment before scaling. The board can then approve resources against evidence rather than treating the initial $2.8 million bridge as an immutable promise.

This proof has underwriting and exit value beyond the first quarter. A disciplined 100-day archive shows future buyers how management identified issues, made decisions, and converted initiatives into reported earnings without double counting. It also reveals whether the sponsor can still earn its return if timing slips or a lever fails. The strongest handoff therefore includes a downside refresh, an exit-value bridge, and a clear cadence for tracking realized EBITDA, cash conversion, and the remaining white space throughout the hold.
